title: 4.1–4.3 Catch-Up

noticeAndWonder.context: Quick review from Lesson 4.3: The arcade leaderboard shows one player scored 150% of the weekly goal, while a rare bonus round only adds a 0.5% point boost. How can a score be more than the whole goal, and how tiny is a 0.5% boost?
wonderStarters: I wonder what would happen if…

revealWordProblem.title: (Review from 4.3) Apply: Power-Up Boost
revealWordProblem.text: In the arcade game, your base score is 80 points. A rare power-up boosts your score to 250% of your base. How many points do you have after the power-up? (Hint: 250% means 2.5 times the base.)
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: 250% = 250 ÷ 100 = 2.5, so 2.5 × 80 = 200 points. Because 250% is greater than 100%, the new score (200) is more than the base score (80).

turnAndTalk.question: The leaderboard shows one player hit 150% of the goal and a bonus round gives a 0.5% boost. How can a percent be more than the whole, and how can one be a tiny sliver?
turnAndTalk.kernel: 150% is more than one whole, and 0.5% is a tiny piece smaller than 1%.

stems.en: ___% means ___ because it is more / less than 100%.
stems.es: ___% significa ___ porque es más / menos que 100%.

stems.en: A percent over 100% means ___, and a percent under 1% means ___.
stems.es: Un porcentaje mayor que 100% significa ___, y uno menor que 1% significa ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students explain 150% is more than one whole (the player beat the goal) and 0.5% is far less than one whole (a tiny boost), connecting to the idea of 100% as the whole.
turnAndTalk.extend: 100% means the whole goal. Explain why scoring 150% does NOT mean the player made an error, but scoring '150% correct on a test' usually would.
extendStems: 150% of a goal makes sense because ___.
150% on a test does not make sense because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: When you wrote percents like 150% and 0.5% as decimals, what did you notice about their size compared to 1?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Percents over 100% become decimals bigger than 1, and percents under 1% become decimals close to 0.

stems.en: Percents over 100% have decimals ___ than 1, and percents under 1% have decimals ___.
stems.es: Los porcentajes mayores que 100% tienen decimales ___ que 1, y los menores que 1% tienen decimales ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students state 150% = 1.5 (greater than 1) and 0.5% = 0.005 (much less than 0.01), and recognize these forms are equivalent.
turnAndTalk.extend: Why does 0.5% turn into 0.005 and not 0.05? Explain the role of dividing by 100, and write 150% as a mixed number too.
extendStems: 150% as a mixed number is ___ because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: A jackpot pays 250% of your tokens and you inserted 40 tokens. One friend says 100 tokens, another says 60. Who is right, and why does '250%' mean more than your tokens?
turnAndTalk.kernel: 250% of 40 is 2.5 times 40, which is 100 tokens.

stems.en: The friend who said ___ tokens is correct because 250% = ___ times the whole.
stems.es: El amigo que dijo ___ fichas tiene razón porque 250% = ___ veces el entero.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students convert 250% to 2.5, multiply 2.5 x 40 = 100, and explain that over 100% means more than the original 40 tokens.
turnAndTalk.extend: The friend who said 60 found 150% of 40. Explain the mistake they likely made, and describe a jackpot percent that WOULD give exactly 40 tokens.
extendStems: You would get exactly 40 tokens when the jackpot is ___% because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice on Percents Greater Than 100% and Less Than 1%, what strategy did you use when a problem felt tricky?
turnAndTalk.kernel: To change any percent to a decimal, divide by 100 (move the decimal point two places to the left).

stems.en: I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.
stems.es: Supe que mi respuesta era razonable porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Listen for students naming a specific strategy tied to 6.AT.4 — not just "I multiplied." They should connect steps to the key idea.
turnAndTalk.extend: How would you help a classmate who made the common mistake from today's lesson? Use one vocabulary word.
extendStems: I would tell them to ___ first because ___.
The mistake happens when you ___ instead of ___.

Read the Big Ideas, warm up with the review problem, then prove you're caught up in the mixed practice.

conceptIntro.heading: The Big Ideas — Lessons 4.1–4.3
conceptIntro.intro: Here is the one thing to remember from each lesson, plus a quick guided example. If one of these feels shaky, that lesson is right above this one in the menu — you can open it any time.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: 4.1: To find a unit rate, divide the total cost by the number of items. The lower cost per item is the better buy. • 4.2: To turn a fraction into a percent, divide the top by the bottom to get a decimal, then multiply by 100. • 4.3: To change any percent to a decimal, divide by 100 (move the decimal point two places to the left).

iDo.title: The Big Ideas (one per lesson)
lines: Lesson 4.1 — Rates and Unit Rates: To find a unit rate, divide the total cost by the number of items. The lower cost per item is the better buy.
Lesson 4.2 — Relate Fractions, Decimals, and Percents: To turn a fraction into a percent, divide the top by the bottom to get a decimal, then multiply by 100.
Lesson 4.3 — Percents Greater Than 100% and Less Than 1%: To change any percent to a decimal, divide by 100 (move the decimal point two places to the left).

explore.instructions: Review from Lesson 4.3: Sort each value into the correct category: Greater than 100%, Between 1% and 100%, or Less than 1%.

discourse.prompt: What do you notice about the decimal form of percents in each category?
discourse.sentenceFrame: Percents greater than 100% have a decimal value ___ than 1, while percents less than 1% have a decimal value ___.

optional.stem: (Lesson 4.1) The Star Blaster cabinet scored 90 points in 3 games. What is the unit rate in points per game?
optional.explanation: Divide points by games: 90 ÷ 3 = 30 points per game.
choiceFeedback: You found 90 × 3 — check: should you multiply or divide to find the rate for one game?
You picked 3 — is that the total points or the points for one game?
You found 90 + 3 — remember, a unit rate comes from dividing, not adding.

optional.stem: (Lesson 4.2) Your arcade scoreboard reads 0.25 of the level cleared. What percent and fraction match this score?
optional.explanation: Move the decimal two places: 0.25 = 25%. As a fraction, 0.25 = 25/100 = 1/4.
choiceFeedback: Remember: multiply the decimal by 100, or move the decimal point right 2 places.
Check your conversion — 0.25 as a percent should be higher.
Double-check your decimal-to-percent conversion.

optional.instructions: (Lesson 4.3) Sort each arcade percent into the right bin: is it less than 1%, between 1% and 100%, or greater than 100%?

approaching.stem: (Lesson 4.1) A booth charges $4.50 for 9 games. What is the unit rate?
choiceFeedback: Double-check your division: $4.50 ÷ 9 — is it $0.45 or $0.50?
Divide the cost by the number of games: $4.50 ÷ 9, not some other operation.
That's the total cost for all 9 games, not the cost for one game.
hints: You know the total cost ($4.50) and the total games (9). A unit rate tells the cost of just ONE game.
To find a unit rate, divide the total cost by the number of games so the second quantity becomes 1.
Set up the division: $4.50 ÷ 9. Think of $4.50 as 450 cents if that makes the division easier.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 4.1) A car travels 180 miles using 6 gallons of gas. What is the unit rate in miles per gallon?
choiceFeedback: That's the number of gallons — you need to divide 180 by 6, not use 6 as the answer.
That's the total miles — divide 180 by 6 to find miles for one gallon.
Check your division: 180 ÷ 6 — is it 30 or 36?
hints: Notice the units in the question: miles PER gallon. That tells you miles go on top and gallons on the bottom.
Divide the total miles by the total gallons so you get the miles for just 1 gallon.
Start the division: 180 ÷ 6. Think: 6 × what number lands on 180?

approaching.instructions: (Lesson 4.2) Sort these values — which are greater than 50% and which are less than 50%?
hints: 50% is the same as 1/2 or 0.5 — that is your comparison line for every card.
Turn each card into a decimal, then ask: is it more or less than 0.5?
Try 3/4 first: 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75. Is 0.75 above or below 0.5? Sort it, then test the other cards the same way.

choiceFeedback: Try again: 3 ÷ 5 × 100.
Divide the numerator by the denominator, then multiply by 100.
Check your calculation.
hints: 3/5 means 3 divided by 5. A percent is just that decimal scaled to 'out of 100'.
Convert fraction → decimal → percent: divide, then multiply the decimal by 100.
Start with 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6. Now move the decimal point two places right to name it as a percent.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 4.3) Which of the following is greater than 100%?
approaching.explanation: 1.25 = 125%, which is greater than 100%. The other values are all less than 1 (less than 100%).
choiceFeedback: A percent greater than 100% is more than a whole.
Review which percents are greater than 100%.
hints: 100% equals exactly 1 whole. A value greater than 100% must be greater than 1.
Rewrite each choice as a decimal and ask: is it more than 1?
Test 0.75 first — it is less than 1, so it is under 100%. Check 3/4, 1.25, and 99/100 the same way.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 4.3) What is 200% written as a decimal?
approaching.explanation: 200% ÷ 100 = 2.0. Percents greater than 100% become decimals greater than 1.
choiceFeedback: Divide 200 by 100, or move the decimal point left 2 places.
200% is twice as much, so the decimal should be 2 point something.
Remember: a percent is per 100.
hints: 200% is more than 100%, so its decimal must be bigger than 1 — that rules out any tiny decimal.
Percent → decimal: divide by 100 (slide the decimal point two places left).
Start at 200. and hop the decimal two places left: 200 → 20.0 → one more hop lands where?

onLevel.instructions: (Lesson 4.1) Complete the table to find unit rates and determine the best deal.
hints: Each pack lists tokens and a total cost. The unit rate column wants the cost of ONE token, like '$0.25 per token'.
Divide the cost by the number of tokens for each pack — dollars ÷ tokens = dollars per token.
For Pack A, divide $5.00 by 20 tokens. Then repeat: $7.00 ÷ 35 for Pack B and $12.50 ÷ 50 for Pack C.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 4.1) Which token pack from the table above is the best deal?
onLevel.explanation: Pack B has a unit rate of $0.20 per token, which is the lowest cost per token.
choiceFeedback: Compare the unit rates: $0.25, $0.20, and $0.25. Are all three the same?
hints: The 'best deal' is the pack where ONE token costs the least — not the pack with the most tokens.
Line up the three unit rates you found in the table and look for the smallest cost per token.
Compare $0.25, $0.20, and $0.25 per token. Which of those is the smallest amount of money?

onLevel.label: (Lesson 4.2) Place each value on the number line: A = 3/8, B = 0.6, C = 85%
hints: The three values are in different forms (fraction, decimal, percent). A number line needs them all in ONE form.
Convert each value to a decimal between 0 and 1, then place it.
Start with A: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375, so A sits between 0.3 and 0.4, closer to 0.4. Now convert 85% the same way.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 4.2) A game shows your score as 7/8 complete. What percent is that?
choiceFeedback: Divide 7 by 8, then multiply by 100.
Convert the fraction to a decimal first.
Check your calculation on the conversion.
hints: 7/8 means 7 divided by 8 — the answer will be a decimal just under 1, so the percent is just under 100%.
Divide the numerator by the denominator, then multiply the decimal by 100 to get the percent.
Compute 7 ÷ 8 = 0.875. Now slide the decimal two places right to read it as a percent.

onLevel.instructions: (Lesson 4.3) Match each value to its equivalent percent.
hints: Every match is the same move: decimal × 100 = percent. Fractions become decimals first (top ÷ bottom).
Multiply each decimal by 100 by sliding the decimal point two places right, then find that percent card.
Start with 1.5: slide the decimal two places right to get its percent. Then 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5 tells you which card 3/2 pairs with.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 4.3) A player scored 0.4% of the bonus points. Which decimal represents this percent?
onLevel.explanation: 0.4% = 0.4 ÷ 100 = 0.004. Move the decimal point two places to the left.
choiceFeedback: Move the decimal point left 2 places in 0.4%.
Check your decimal conversion carefully.
hints: 0.4% is less than 1%, so the matching decimal must be smaller than 0.01.
Divide the percent by 100: the decimal point moves two places left, and zeros fill the gaps.
Start at 0.4 and hop the decimal left twice: 0.4 → 0.04 → one more hop gives the answer's form.

extending.title: (Lesson 4.1) Find the Rate Error

workedExample.label: Find the unit rate: 12 tickets for $8
Write the unit rate
workedExample.work: The unit rate is $1.50 per ticket

extending.correctWork: To find cost per ticket, divide $8 ÷ 12 = $0.67 per ticket (rounded). The student divided tickets by cost instead of cost by tickets.
hints: What should go in the numerator — the cost or the tickets?
To find 'dollars per ticket,' divide dollars by tickets: $8 ÷ 12 ≈ $0.67 per ticket.

extending.title: (Lesson 4.2) Find the Conversion Error
hints: 2 ÷ 3 doesn't terminate — is 0.67 the exact decimal?
0.67 is rounded. The precise decimal is 0.666... (repeating), making the percent 66.7% or 66⅔%.

extending.title: (Lesson 4.3) Find the Percent Error

workedExample.label: Move the decimal two places left

extending.correctWork: 0.6% means 0.6 out of 100. Move the decimal two places left: 0.6 → 0.006. The correct answer is 0.6% = 0.006.
hints: The student only moved the decimal one place instead of two.
0.6% is less than 1%, so the decimal must be less than 0.01. 0.06 is too large.

optionalActivity.name: Catch-Up Challenge
optionalActivity.intro: Mix it up: pick the right lesson's big idea for each problem — that's the real catch-up skill.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Percents Greater Than 100% and Less Than 1% is treating every percent-to-decimal conversion the same way regardless of size — for example, writing 150% as 0.15 (as if it were an ordinary under-100% percent) instead of 1.5, or writing 0.5% as 0.5 (forgetting to divide by 100 at all) instead of 0.005. Before finalizing an answer, check that the decimal for any percent over 100% is greater than 1, and the decimal for any percent under 1% is less than 0.01.

diagram.title: 300% Jackpot of 30 Tokens
diagram.caption: The top bar is your 30 tokens (100% = one whole); the jackpot bar stacks three 30-token wholes, so 300% = 90 tokens — more than what you put in.

connect.scenario: A different arcade machine pays a jackpot of 300% of your tokens if you win. You inserted 30 tokens. One friend says the jackpot is 90 tokens. Another friend says it's 33 tokens.
connect.promptQuestion: Who is correct, and how many tokens does the jackpot pay?
connect.prompt: The friend who said ___ tokens is correct because 300% of 30 = ___ × 30 = ___. The other friend treated 300% as if it were ___% instead.

exitTicket.stem: (Catch-up check, from Lesson 4.2) Which shows 0.45 as a fraction and a percent?
choiceFeedback: Try converting 0.45 to a fraction and percent differently.
Check: 0.45 as a fraction should be 45/100, and as a percent is 45%.
Look at both the fraction and percent for each option.
hints: 0.45 is 'forty-five hundredths' — that phrase hands you both the fraction AND the percent.
Write 0.45 over 100 as a fraction and simplify; for the percent, multiply the decimal by 100. Check that a choice matches BOTH.
Start with 45/100 and divide top and bottom by 5. Then compute 0.45 × 100 for the percent, and match both parts.
